covers.quote: The full names of mountains, rivers, valleys, bays, islands and other features always take initial capitals.
Some shortened forms that are popular names or nicknames are also capitalised.
Keep the initial capital when the general term is a well-recognised abbreviation and works as a proper name.
use initial capitals.

parts.quote: the Hunter Valley
the Three Sisters
the Paroo River
The Snowy Mountains can also be called the ‘Snowies’.
The northern part of the Northern Territory is known as the ‘Top End’.
The Great Barrier Reef is also called ‘the Reef’.
The Gulf of Carpentaria is also known as ‘the Gulf’.
Mt Tennent is part of Namadgi National Park.

rules.violation_condition: An official topographic name or an established proper-name shortened form lacks its required initial capitals.
when: Applies to the full names of mountains, rivers, valleys, bays, islands and other topographic features.
Also applies to established popular names and nicknames that are capitalised as proper names.
A well-recognised shortened generic term retains its capital when it works as a proper name, such as ‘the Reef’.
The mountain abbreviation ‘Mt’ takes an initial capital.
rules.why: G-2 consolidates the full-name and established shortened-name cases into one capitalisation check; G-4 absorbs their restatements.

covers.quote: Write generic terms in lower case
When using the same generic term for 2 or more names in the same sentence, use lower case for the generic term.
Don’t use an initial capital if you’re using the noun in a generic sense.

parts.quote: I paddled a kayak 200 km down the Balonne River. The river was in flood for some of the trip.
The Barossa and Hunter valleys are important winemaking areas.
The Barossa Valley is in South Australia and the Hunter Valley is in New South Wales.
The Amazon rainforest is vital to the health of our planet.

rules.quote: In most cases, don’t use initial capitals when you use the name as a generic term.
rules.violation_condition: A topographic term has an initial capital even though it is used generically rather than as part of a proper name.
when: Includes a generic reference back to a named feature, such as ‘the river’.
Includes a generic term shared by 2 or more names in the same sentence.
Includes a generic noun following a name when that noun is not part of the official name.
Does not apply when the term is a well-recognised shortened form functioning as a proper name.
Does not remove capitals from a term that remains part of each separately written proper name.
rules.why: G-2 treats generic references, shared generic terms and unofficial descriptors as cases of the same check; the proper-name exception limits that check.

parts.quote: Mt Tennent is part of Namadgi National Park.

rules.quote: Use the abbreviation consistently in content
rules.specification: Interpret consistency as using the same choice, ‘Mt’ or ‘Mount’, for mountain names throughout a content item once the abbreviation is adopted. The page does not explicitly define the scope of consistency.
rules.violation_condition: Content uses ‘Mt’ for mountain names but inconsistently switches between abbreviated ‘Mt’ and spelled-out ‘Mount’.
when: Applies when the content uses the mountain abbreviation ‘Mt’.
The sentence specifically discusses ‘Mt’; it does not explicitly establish a consistency rule for every topographic abbreviation.
rules.why: The consistency requirement is distinct from capitalisation; G-4 keeps the latter with the existing capitalisation rule.

covers.quote: Spell out the names of other topographic features if you can.

rules.quote: Use the abbreviated form only where there’s limited space or a lot of repetition, such as in tables and maps.
rules.specification: The page does not define how much repetition is ‘a lot’ or how to establish that space is limited. Those conditions require editorial judgement.
rules.violation_condition: A topographic feature other than a mountain is abbreviated where neither limited space nor substantial repetition justifies the abbreviation.
when: Applies to topographic features other than mountains using ‘Mt’.
Abbreviation is permitted where space is limited or there is a lot of repetition.
Tables and maps are examples of contexts that may justify abbreviation, not an exhaustive list.
rules.why: G-2 combines the spelling-out instruction with its limited-space and repetition exceptions.

when: Applies when a topographic feature term is abbreviated.
rules.why: The authorised form is a separate lookup check from whether abbreviation is justified.

rules.quote: Don’t use an apostrophe for possessive names
rules.violation_condition: A topographic name contains an apostrophe inserted to mark an apparent possessive.
when: Applies to possessive-looking elements within topographic names.
The explanatory statement that place names do not usually include punctuation is not a blanket prohibition on every punctuation mark.
rules.why: G-4 combines the heading and body instruction; E-2 attaches the explicit Correct/Incorrect pair to this prohibition.

covers.quote: Spell the plural form correctly

parts.quote: There are 4 Mount Wellingtons in Australia but only one Mount Coot-tha.

rules.quote: The plural of any topographic name is formed simply by adding ‘s’ or ‘es’.
rules.violation_condition: A plural topographic name is formed by something other than adding the appropriate ‘s’ or ‘es’ ending to the name.
when: Applies when referring to multiple places bearing the same topographic name.
rules.why: G-4 selects the actionable body wording rather than the vague heading.

rules.quote: Write compass points in lower case
rules.violation_condition: A spelled-out compass point used as a direction has an unnecessary capital letter.
when: Applies to spelled-out compass directions in text, including directional forms such as ‘north-westerly’.
Does not apply to compass-point initialisms used in tables, illustrations and some specialist works.
Does not treat the capitalisation of an official geographic name as directional capitalisation.
An ordinary sentence-initial capital is not an unnecessary compass-point capital.
rules.why: G-4 combines the heading and restatement; G-3 records the initialism permission as an exception rather than a separate rule.

parts.quote: north-east
west-north-west
A north-westerly wind was blowing the fire towards the town.

rules.quote: Use hyphens for points such as ‘north-east’.
rules.violation_condition: A spelled-out compound compass point lacks a hyphen between its directional components.
when: Applies to compound compass points and their directional forms, such as ‘north-east’, ‘west-north-west’ and ‘north-westerly’.
Does not apply to compass-point initialisms, which have no hyphens.
rules.why: Missing hyphens are a distinct violation from unnecessary capitals, so the two instructions are separate checks.

rules.violation_condition: A compass-point initialism contains a lowercase letter instead of the required capital letter.
when: Applies to compass-point initialisms.
The page permits these initialisms in tables, illustrations and some specialist works.
rules.why: The capital-letter requirement is separate from the punctuation prohibition; G-3 keeps the permission as context.

rules.violation_condition: A compass-point initialism contains a full stop or hyphen.
when: Applies to compass-point initialisms.
The page permits these initialisms in tables, illustrations and some specialist works.
A sentence-ending full stop after an initialism is not punctuation within the initialism.
rules.why: Full stops and hyphens are cases of the same internal-punctuation prohibition, distinct from letter case.
